articles.title: Kashmir: Emerging Complexities
articles.description: Kashmir’s socio-political landscape has long been shaped by overlapping layers of sovereignty, geography, ethnicity, language, religion and community. These have historically produced entrenched power
articles.html:
Kashmir’s socio-political landscape has long been shaped by overlapping layers of sovereignty, geography, ethnicity, language, religion and community. These have historically produced entrenched power structures in politics, bureaucracy, and society, privileged certain groups while marginalising others.
While the new political and governance framework has papered over Kashmir’s historically inherited complexities, it is also reigniting and reconfiguring the dormant ones. Shared sovereignty and concentrated elite power are giving way to a more plural but contested arena in which sub-ethnic groups are asserting agency. 

The governance changes have reshaped power dynamics in J&K, particularly through the politicization of sub-ethnic identities. The quasi-sovereign framework under Article 370 had insulated and entrenched a Valley-centric Kashmiri Muslim elite hegemony. Its removal has dismantled that insulation. Alongside, in its place, new avenues have opened for previously peripheral groups, notably sub-ethnic tribal communities through delimitation, political reservations for Scheduled Tribes (STs), extension of central schemes and expanded affirmative action.

Far from simplifying the region’s challenges, this shift has layered fresh complexities onto an already fragmented terrain, reshaping power contestation and raising new questions about social cohesion. While this could foster long-term equity, the immediate outcome is greater fragmentation, with additional layers of competition over political seats, administrative roles, employment opportunities, economic resources, and social recognition.

The recent affirmative action policy has institutionalised and amplified sub-ethnic distinctions within the population of Jammu and Kashmir, particularly the demographic majority. Conferring the Gujjars and Bakarwals with dedicated channels for reservations in education, employment, and political representation has deepened the divide. So too the subsequent policy shifts, particularly the extension of Scheduled Tribe status to the Pahari ethnic group. All these policy changes have intensified competitive claims over finite reservation quotas and electoral constituencies.

Prior to independence, the Dogra monarch governed a Muslim-majority population, with sharp regional contrasts: the Kashmiri-speaking Muslim-majority Kashmir Valley, the Dogri-speaking Jammu region with its Hindu plurality, and Buddhist-majority Ladakh. Linguistic diversity intersected with communal identities, creating a mosaic prone to segmentation within and across regions.

Post-independence and accession, the shared sovereignty and constitutional status allowed local elites, primarily Valley-centric Kashmiri Muslims linked to the National Conference and successor parties, to consolidate and retain political power. Land reforms redistributed feudal holdings but often channelled benefits toward politically aligned groups. Social power reinforced hierarchies as nomadic and tribal communities, including Gujjars and Bakarwals, remained on the margins. Traditional power structures thus sustained a Valley-elite hegemony intertwined with communal and regional imbalances.

The J&K Reorganisation Act fundamentally altered this architecture. The 2022 Delimitation Commission redrew constituencies, expanding the proposed Assembly to 90 seats: 43 in Jammu and 47 in the Kashmir Valley. Most significantly, it reserved nine seats for Scheduled Tribes — six in Jammu division and three in the Valley. This marked the first formal political reservation for STs in the region’s legislative history. Seven seats were also reserved for Scheduled Castes in Jammu.

Extension of the Forest Rights Act and other central welfare schemes further opened administrative and economic pathways. Sub-ethnic tribal identity rooted in nomadic pastoralism and the Gojri language transitioned from being peripheral to becoming strategically empowered within the new governance framework.
Thus, Gujjars and Bakarwals have emerged as primary beneficiaries. As the third-largest ethnic group and the bulk of the pre-2019 Scheduled Tribe population, they gained guaranteed Assembly representation and influence in local bodies. Post-delimitation elections saw dozens of Gujjar-Bakarwal candidates elected to District Development Councils and Block Development Councils, including several chairpersons.

This empowerment, however, introduced immediate tensions. When the Centre granted Scheduled Tribe status to additional communities, including Paharis, Gujjar-Bakarwal groups protested strongly, fearing dilution of their existing quota in jobs and education. The administration created a supplementary category for new groups, raising the total ST reservation share. Yet competition over political influence in reserved constituencies and welfare allocations persists. Sub-ethnic assertions now compete even within the tribal category, adding layers atop older Valley-Jammu or communal divides.
The integration of Gujjars, Bakarwals, and other tribal communities into the emerging power structure carries mixed implications. Positively, it advances inclusion for historically disadvantaged nomadic and hill communities through political reservations, job and education quotas, and schemes such as the Forest Rights Act. This enables stronger advocacy for education, healthcare, grazing rights, and infrastructure in remote areas, improves intergenerational mobility, and broadens notions of belonging beyond traditional Valley-centric narratives — a meaningful step toward democratisation in a conflict-scarred region.The Pir Panchal belt, comprising Rajouri and Poonch districts, has emerged as a power centre for these communities. This is distinct from the Kashmir Valley’s traditional dominance or the core Jammu-Samba-Kathua Hindu-majority belt.

However, these gains intensify overall complexity and risk social cohesion. This institutionalisation of sub-ethnic distinctions has created new fault lines between Gujjars-Bakarwals and Paharis over quota shares and control of reserved constituencies. Intra-tribal competition now overlays older Valley-Jammu and communal divides. Resource competition over forests, migration routes, and development funds risks exacerbating frictions in sensitive border districts, potentially fuelling intra-community or hill-region polarisation.

These changes do not merely reflect or accentuate pre-existing realities; they actively incentivise the strategic mobilisation and boundary-maintenance of differentiated identities. Sub-ethnic groups now articulate claims primarily to secure or safeguard access to state resources — jobs, education quotas, political seats, and welfare benefits — thereby transforming historically fluid or overlapping affiliations into more rigid and politically salient categories.
As a result, broader religious and regional solidarities among Muslims are increasingly mediated, and often subordinated, by sub-ethnic competition. This process is most visible in districts such as Rajouri and Poonch, where overlapping claims to tribal status and reservation benefits have sharpened inter-community tensions. The overall effect furthers the trend in which the demographic majority risks being reduced to a political minority in access to power and resources, contributing to greater social differentiation and political fragmentation.

Broader social well-being suffers from heightened identity-based mobilisation: politics fragments along sub-ethnic, regional, and quota lines rather than converging on shared development or reconciliation. This multiplies contesting interests and complicates consensus on governance and peace.
The reconfiguration has amplified the visibility of ST-reserved politics and local patronage. These sub-ethnic identities intersect with regional nuances where power has long been mediated through clan and family networks rather than purely ideological or party lines. Prominent families within Gujjar and related tribal/Pahari ecosystems have consolidated influence through a blend of spiritual authority, political brokerage, land/pastoral networks, and post-2019 quota gains.

This power shift directly maps and exemplifies the ongoing reservation crisis. The earlier expansion of reservations, including the 10% ST quota for the Pahari-speaking group, contributed to pushing open merit down to around 30%, sparking widespread protests in the Valley by general-category aspirants. The Omar Abdullah government’s Cabinet Sub-Committee review and subsequent decision to rationalise by trimming EWS and RBA quotas is an attempt to address Valley grievances, yet it immediately triggers counter-mobilisation from reserved groups fearing dilution. Hence the dithering and the delay.
Social well-being in Kashmir now depends on managing these new dynamics without reigniting older divides. Effective institutions must balance inclusion with cross-community mechanisms; otherwise, complexity risks breeding instability rather than resilience. The region’s trajectory hinges on navigating this intricate ethnic-geographic tapestry with foresight and fairness.


The author is a Contributing Editor of Greater Kashmir.

articles.title: Building Bridges
articles.description: The recent repatriation of Zeeshan Ahmad Mir at the Kaman Post in Uri highlights the persistent, deeply human cost of a divided Jammu and Kashmir. When Zeeshan crossed the Line of Control (LoC) from P
articles.html:
The recent repatriation of Zeeshan Ahmad Mir at the Kaman Post in Uri highlights the persistent, deeply human cost of a divided Jammu and Kashmir. When Zeeshan crossed the Line of Control (LoC) from Pankedi village to meet Iram Majeed, his journey—driven by a Snapchat romance and a desire to escape an arranged marriage—illustrated how a heavily fortified geopolitical boundary abruptly fractures everyday human relationships, shared cultures, and family lineages. 

The Operation Sindoor in May 2025 fundamentally altered the bilateral dynamics. India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance during the operation signalled a major shift: using vital water resources of the western rivers (Jhelum and Chenab) as a strategic lever against cross-border terrorism. This move severely pressured Pakistan’s agricultural economy and signalled that India is willing to dismantle long-standing bilateral frameworks to enforce national security. 

While Pakistan maintains a close strategic relationship with China (anchored by the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor) and seeks to sustain historical security ties with the US, these relationships face major constraints: China’s primary interest remains protecting its investments and maintaining stability along its trade corridors rather than backing aggressive territorial shifts that could trigger a wider conflict. The US views its relationship with India as a vital pillar of its broader Indo-Pacific strategy. Consequently, Washington consistently advocates for a peaceful, bilateral resolution between New Delhi and Islamabad rather than endorsing territorial revisions.

Is Realignment Post-2026 Possible?
India’s formal integration of Jammu and Kashmir following the 2019 constitutional changes, coupled with its post-operation Sindoor stance on cross-border security, has effectively closed the door on territorial concessions. Furthermore, the immense economic instability within Pakistan limits its capacity to project power or force as a means of rewriting the borders.

While geopolitical shifts dominate national headlines, the true transformation along the Line of Control (LoC) is taking place on the ground. For decades, frontier sectors like Uri, Keran, Gurez, and Poonch were defined solely by military gridlines, shelling, and isolated economies. Today, a paradigm shift is transforming these border areas from tense conflict zones into active drivers of regional economic growth. The macro-economic data reflects this structural turnaround. The Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) of Jammu and Kashmir has reached approximately ₹2.86 lakh crore, growing at a steady real rate of 5.82%. This economic resilience is directly impacting the livelihoods of border communities through three major pillars.

The most visible economic transformation is the deliberate opening and promotion of Border Tourism. Places that were once strictly off-limits to civilians are now witnessing unprecedented footfall. The Kaman Post Surge: Located right at the Kaman Post in the Uri sector—near the historic Aman Setu (Peace Bridge) where Zeeshan was repatriated—hundreds of domestic tourists are now visiting monthly and the number is increasing. The area has seen integrated infrastructural upgrades, including the Wall of Valour, the Setu Selfie Point, visitor canteens, and local souvenir shops managed by residents.
The ₹8-Crore Uri Infrastructure Plan: To sustain this momentum, the government has launched a dedicated tourism development framework. This includes constructing a Tourism Facilitation Centre in Uri town, establishing eco-friendly tourist huts and trekking trails in Bosiyan-Gingal and Chotali, and creating a riverfront park at Mohra. This infrastructure ensures that tourist spending directly benefits local homestays, transport operators, and guides. For generations, border farmers were restricted to subsistence farming due to erratic security conditions. The current stability has allowed for the implementation of high-value agricultural projects: Holistic Agriculture Development programs are actively shifting local economies toward high-value, organic, and exotic crops. Horticulture has seen an overall production expansion of 12.5%, with almond and walnut exports from the region reaching significant values. The establishment of thousands of Kisan Khidmat Ghars (Agri-Business Centres) and the linking of local agrarian markets (mandis) to national digital portals mean that a farmer in a remote corner of Uri can now command competitive, real-time national prices for their produce, bypassing exploitative middlemen

Historically, the lack of private-sector employment left border youth with limited economic avenues, often feeding undercurrents of unrest. Through state-sponsored credit-linked livelihood schemes, thousands of new micro-enterprises and self-employment units have been established in the frontier districts, absorbing over 85,000 youth into the mainstream economy. 

This is supported by a robust expansion of rural banking infrastructure and specialized employment initiatives aimed at incubating grass-roots businesses in logistics, hospitality, and handlooms. This economic revival provides a tangible answer to the “way out” of the historical impasse. When border villages are economically thriving, connected by high-speed digital networks, and welcoming visitors from across the nation, the psychological sense of isolation begins to dissolve. By prioritizing local economic security, infrastructure, and human welfare, the region is showing that even while political borders remain fixed, the human and financial isolation of the past can be systematically overcome.

The way forward: 
It requires moving past 20th-century political impasses to focus on economic integration and humanitarian dignity along the Line of Control (LoC).First, the region must scale its “Border Dividend.” Sustaining Jammu and Kashmir’s 5.82% GSDP growth means establishing localized processing zones for high-value frontier produce like walnuts and saffron, while utilizing state-backed micro-loans to expand resident-owned border homestays. Deepening all-weather road tunnels and 5G connectivity will permanently dissolve geographical isolation for frontier youth. Second, the deeply human cost of the divide must be managed via institutionalized compassion. Standardized protocols should be established for the swift, dignified repatriation of non-hostile, inadvertent border crossers within 72 hours. Furthermore, highly vetted, secure “Humanitarian Corridors” at designated points like the Kaman Post could allow strictly verified divided families to meet without requiring complex international visas. Finally, future engagement should pivot toward ecological diplomacy. Joint data-sharing on climate vulnerabilities—such as melting Himalayan glaciers and flash floods—offers a neutral, non-political framework for stability.

By prioritizing local prosperity and structured human compassion, the LoC can transform from an active wound into a peaceful, stable frontier.

Prof. Upendra Kaul, Founder Director Gauri Kaul Foundation

articles.title: Water Problems in Rural Areas
articles.description: In rural areas, we see water, yet there is no drop to drink. The problem does not stem from the consumers, scarcity, or water consumption, but from the unaccountable use of water. We cannot define the
articles.html:
In rural areas, we see water, yet there is no drop to drink. The problem does not stem from the consumers, scarcity, or water consumption, but from the unaccountable use of water. We cannot define the importance of water in simple words. It is life itself, and this vital resource, upon which all life depends, is wasted due to mismanagement and improper use and lack of proper mechanisms.

How we can provide neat and clean water to every household in Kashmir is a question addressed by many policies. We will also help by suggesting some solutions for water conservation, filtration, supply to all households, and possible remedies based on our local experience.
Currently, there is no government fee or meter for tap water consumption in rural areas, which leads to misuse of water and scarcity in towns and cities. Secondly, there was a time when we drank and used stream and Nallah water, but this has been completely disturbed due to mining and crusher dust. This type of water has now been heavily polluted and is no longer in use. Illegal sand extraction continues despite Supreme Court bans, such as in Nalla Mawer, disrupting the natural flow of local streams disrupts the water level and its cleanliness. 

Thirdly, water management scheme is not implemented in villages, where the actual water comes. Through streams are often polluted with waste on to the shores of streams and the flow of these streams becomes dirty. Often, we see locals in villages put up their cow dog, waste either on the side of the road or at the banks of river or stream. This practice must be barred by the local administration and keeping these streams clean should be promoted.
Fourthly, encroachment on natural water bodies is a serious problem. People have constructed houses on the banks of rivers, lakes. Jammu and Kashmir have abundant water resources like rivers, lakes, ponds, and streams that could provide 24-hour drinking water supply, but poor management, mechanisms, encroachment, and illegal use prevent this. For example, people in Sopore lack regular tap water supply despite being very close to Wular Lake, India’s first lake producing crystal-clear water. Proper use of Wular alone could supply all of Kashmir.

Fifthly, Kashmir lacks sufficient filtration plants, and water reuse is not practiced. Separating drinking water from agricultural water supply could be done even with local filtration plants. At local levels tap water is used in agricultural supplies. 

At the end of the day, water problems cannot be solved by the government alone. Local consumers must take steps forward. Borewell culture and wells exist in some places, but it has not been made a regular practice. Even in some villages, voluntary tubewells can help cater water to hundreds of families jointly. One tubewell can serve a maximum of 20 families through water motors with joint connections. Tap water should not be wasted on agriculture or washing cars at home. Thousands of villages lack water, but metered water usage and better management can provide water to every home. Helping the government manage village water use and identifying where water is wasted or polluted due to illegal mining is essential.

The water level is decreasing day by day due to illegal encroachment, mismanagement, unaccountable use of water, misuse of water, and lack of proper mechanisms. At the ground level, we have not seen any policies aimed at providing fresh water and stopping water misuse. A local policy is needed that includes local stakeholders, which has never been done. Involving local stakeholders will help the government frame better policies suited to their needs. We should utilize the experience of grassroots level people to address and implement solutions at the grassroots level for the benefit of the community by the government.
